one_sentence_failure_summary: The agent repeatedly implements brittle global motion heuristics instead of proper spatial trajectory tracking to detect takeoff and landing events, and then accepts obviously wrong end-of-video frames (106, 119 out of 120) as correct after only verifying output file format rather than frame accuracy.
t_err_evidence: Step 7: Agent writes jump_analyzer.py using global mean intensity differences from background as the motion signal, which cannot distinguish approach/run from actual jump airborne phase; the algorithm design is fundamentally flawed from the start for detecting specific jump events.
t_commit_evidence: Step 20: Agent reads output.toml showing takeoff=106, land=119 (very end of 120-frame video) and declares 'The results look reasonable now', accepting the wrong output and moving to create a format-only test rather than questioning the suspicious near-end-of-video frames.
t_surface_evidence: Step 13: Revised script detects motion only in frames 110-119 (last 10 of 120 frames) with peak at frame 110, which is a clear observable signal that the algorithm is detecting athlete exit or end-of-video content rather than the actual hurdle jump event.
trigger_explanation: The agent lacks the domain knowledge that detecting specific athletic events like hurdle jump takeoff/landing requires spatial analysis (e.g., tracking athlete bounding box vertical position over time) rather than global frame intensity or motion heuristics. All four script versions rely on frame-mean differences that conflate any motion (athlete running into frame, camera shake) with the specific jump event.
forewarning_evidence: Step 13: Motion only detected in frames 110-119 out of 120 total frames, suggesting the algorithm is detecting near-end activity rather than the jump. Step 17: Results span frames 5-119 (essentially the entire video), showing the threshold is meaningless. Both outputs indicate the heuristic is not meaningfully discriminating the jump event.
